title: Book 5, Chapter 15 — Tenth Year of the War—Death of Cleon and Brasidas—Peace of Nicias
paragraphs: The next summer the year-long truce ended, having lasted until the Pythian games. During the armistice the Athenians expelled the Delians from Delos, concluding that they must have been polluted by some old offence at the time of their consecration, and that this had been the omission in the previous purification of the island, which, as I have related, had been thought to have been duly accomplished by the removal of the graves of the dead. Pharnaces gave the Delians Atramyttium in Asia, and they settled there after leaving Delos.

Meanwhile Cleon persuaded the Athenians to let him sail, at the end of the armistice, against the towns in the direction of Thrace. He took with him twelve hundred heavy infantry and three hundred horse from Athens, a large force of allies, and thirty ships. He first put in at Scione, which was still under siege, picked up some heavy infantry from the army there, and then sailed into Cophos, a harbor in the territory of Torone, not far from the town. From there, having learned from deserters that Brasidas was not in Torone and that the garrison was not strong enough to face him in battle, he advanced with his army on the town and sent ten ships to sail around into the harbor. He came first to the fortification recently thrown up in front of the town by Brasidas to enclose the suburb — for which he had pulled down part of the original wall and made the whole into a single city. To this point Pasitelidas, the Lacedaemonian commander, hurried with what garrison there was, to repel the Athenian assault. But finding himself hard pressed, and seeing the ships that had been sent around sailing into the harbor, Pasitelidas began to fear that they might reach the city before its defenders, and that, with the fortification taken as well, he might be captured. He abandoned the outwork and ran back into the town. But the Athenians from the ships had already taken Torone, and the land force, following at his heels, burst in with him in a rush over the part of the old wall that had been pulled down. They killed some of the Peloponnesians and Toronaeans in the melee and took the rest prisoner, including Pasitelidas the commander. Brasidas meanwhile had advanced to relieve Torone, and had only about four miles to go when he heard on the road that the town had fallen, and turned back. Cleon and the Athenians set up two trophies, one by the harbor and the other by the fortification. They enslaved the wives and children of the Toronaeans, and sent the men, together with the Peloponnesians and any Chalcidians present, to the number of seven hundred, off to Athens. From there they all eventually came home: the Peloponnesians on the conclusion of peace, and the rest by being exchanged against other prisoners with the Olynthians. About the same time Panactum, a fortress on the Athenian border, was taken by treachery by the Boeotians. Meanwhile Cleon, after placing a garrison in Torone, weighed anchor and sailed around Athos on his way to Amphipolis.

About the same time, Phaeax son of Erasistratus set sail with two colleagues as ambassador from Athens to Italy and Sicily. After the Athenians had left Sicily on the pacification, the Leontines had enrolled a number of new citizens, and the commons had a plan to redivide the land. The upper classes, aware of this, called in the Syracusans and expelled the commons. The commons were scattered in various directions, while the upper classes came to an agreement with the Syracusans, abandoned and laid waste their own city, and went to live in Syracuse, where they were made citizens. Afterwards some of them grew dissatisfied. They left Syracuse and occupied Phocaeae, a quarter of the town of Leontini, and Bricinniae, a strong place in Leontine territory. There, joined by most of the exiled commons, they carried on the war from these fortifications. The Athenians, hearing of this, sent Phaeax to see whether he could somehow convince their allies there and the rest of the Sicilians of the ambitious designs of Syracuse, and induce them to form a general coalition against her, and so save the commons of Leontini. Once in Sicily, Phaeax succeeded at Camarina and Agrigentum, but was rebuffed at Gela, and so did not go on to the rest, since he saw he would not succeed with them. He returned through the country of the Sicels to Catana, visiting Bricinniae on the way and encouraging its inhabitants, and then sailed back to Athens.

On his voyage along the coast to and from Sicily, he negotiated with some cities in Italy on the matter of friendship with Athens. He also fell in with some Locrian settlers exiled from Messina. They had been sent there when the Locrians were called in by one of the factions that divided Messina after the pacification of Sicily, and Messina came for a time into the hands of the Locrians. Meeting these settlers on their way home, Phaeax did them no harm, since the Locrians had agreed with him for a treaty with Athens. They were the only one of the allies that had not made peace with Athens at the time of the reconciliation among the Sicilians. Indeed, they would not have done so even now if they had not been pressed by a war with the Hipponians and Medmaeans on their border, who were colonists of theirs. Phaeax meanwhile continued on his voyage and at last arrived at Athens.

Cleon, whom we left on his voyage from Torone to Amphipolis, made Eion his base. After an unsuccessful assault on the Andrian colony of Stagirus, he took Galepsus, a colony of Thasos, by storm. He now sent envoys to Perdiccas to require his attendance with an army, as the alliance provided, and others to Thrace, to Polles, king of the Odomantians, who was to bring as many Thracian mercenaries as possible. He himself remained inactive at Eion, awaiting their arrival. Informed of this, Brasidas in turn took up a position of observation on Cerdylium, a place on high ground in Argilian territory across the river, not far from Amphipolis. It commanded a view in every direction, so that Cleon's army could not move without his seeing it; for he fully expected that Cleon, despising the small numbers of his opponent, would march against Amphipolis with the force he already had with him. At the same time Brasidas made his preparations, calling to his standard fifteen hundred Thracian mercenaries and all the Edonians, both horse and targeteers. He also had a thousand Myrcinian and Chalcidian targeteers, in addition to those in Amphipolis, and a force of heavy infantry numbering altogether about two thousand, plus three hundred Hellenic horse. Of these, fifteen hundred he had with him on Cerdylium; the rest were stationed with Clearidas in Amphipolis.

After remaining quiet for some time, Cleon was at last forced to do as Brasidas expected. His soldiers, tired of their inactivity, also began seriously to reflect on the weakness and incompetence of their commander, on the skill and courage that would be opposed to him, and on their own original unwillingness to come along with him. When these grumblings reached Cleon's ears, he resolved not to disgust the army by keeping it in the same place, and broke camp and advanced. The general's mood was what it had been at Pylos: his success there had given him confidence in his own ability. He never imagined that anyone would come out to fight him, and said that he was rather going up to inspect the place. If he was waiting for his reinforcements, it was not in order to make victory secure should he be forced to engage, but to be able to surround and storm the city. Accordingly he came up and posted his army on a strong hill in front of Amphipolis, and proceeded to examine the lake formed by the Strymon, and how the town lay on the side of Thrace. He thought he could withdraw at his leisure without fighting, since no one was visible on the wall or coming out of the gates, all of which were shut. Indeed, it seemed a mistake not to have brought siege engines with him: he could then have taken the town, with no one to defend it.

As soon as Brasidas saw the Athenians on the move, he came down himself from Cerdylium and entered Amphipolis. He did not venture to march out in regular order against the Athenians: he distrusted his own strength and thought it inadequate to the attempt — not in numbers, since these were not so unequal, but in quality, since the flower of the Athenian army was in the field, with the best of the Lemnians and Imbrians. So he prepared to attack them by stratagem. He thought that by showing the enemy the size of his force and the makeshifts he had been put to in arming it, he would have less chance of beating them than by keeping them out of sight, and so making them realize how good a reason he had to be despised. Accordingly he picked out a hundred and fifty heavy infantry, and putting the rest under Clearidas, decided to attack suddenly, before the Athenians withdrew. He thought he would not have another chance of catching them alone if their reinforcements were once allowed to come up. So he called all his soldiers together to encourage them and explain his intention, and spoke as follows:

"Peloponnesians, the character of the country we come from — one that has always owed its freedom to courage — and the fact that you are Dorians, while the enemy you are about to fight are Ionians whom you are accustomed to beat, are things that need no further comment. But the plan of attack I propose to follow is worth explaining, so that the fact that we are venturing out with a part rather than the whole of our forces does not damp your courage by the apparent disadvantage it puts you in. I imagine it is the poor opinion he has of us, and the fact that he has no idea of anyone coming out to engage him, that has made the enemy march up to the place and look carelessly about, as he is doing, without noticing us. But the most successful soldier will always be the one who most readily detects a blunder of this kind, and who, carefully measuring his own resources, makes his attack not so much by open and regular approaches as by seizing the moment. These stratagems, which give the greatest service to our friends by most completely deceiving our enemies, have the most brilliant name in war. Therefore, while their careless confidence lasts, and while they are still thinking — as in my judgment they are now doing — more of retreat than of holding their position, while their spirit is slack and not strung tight with expectation, I, with the men under my command, will, if possible, take them by surprise and fall at a run upon their center. After that, Clearidas, when you see me already on top of them and, as is likely, spreading panic among them, take with you the Amphipolitans and the rest of the allies, suddenly open the gates and rush out, and engage them as quickly as you can. That is our best chance of producing panic among them, since a fresh attacker has always more terror for an enemy than the one he is already engaged with. Show yourself a brave man, as a Spartan should. And you, allies, follow him like men, and remember that zeal, honor, and obedience mark the good soldier, and that this day will make you either free men and allies of Lacedaemon, or slaves of Athens. Even if you escape without personal loss of liberty or life, your bondage will be on harsher terms than before, and you will also hold up the liberation of the rest of the Hellenes. So no cowardice on your part, seeing the greatness of what is at stake — and I will show that what I preach to others I can practice myself."

After this brief speech, Brasidas himself prepared for the sortie and placed the rest of the troops, with Clearidas, at the Thracian gates to support him as agreed. Meanwhile he had been seen coming down from Cerdylium, and then in the city — which is overlooked from outside — sacrificing near the temple of Athene. In short, all his movements had been observed, and word was brought to Cleon, who had at that moment gone forward to look around, that the whole of the enemy's force could be seen in the town and that the feet of large numbers of horses and men were visible under the gates, as if a sortie were intended. On hearing this he went up to look. Having done so, and being unwilling to venture on the decisive step of battle before his reinforcements came up, and supposing he would have time to retire, he ordered the retreat to be sounded and sent orders to the men to carry it out by moving on the left wing in the direction of Eion — which was, in fact, the only way they could go. This was not quick enough for him, however, so he joined the retreat in person and made the right wing wheel around, exposing its unarmed side to the enemy. It was then that Brasidas, seeing the Athenian force in motion and his opportunity come, said to the men with him and the rest: "Those fellows will never stand before us — you can see it by the way their spears and heads are bobbing. Troops that do that seldom stand a charge. Quick, someone, open the gates I spoke of, and let us be out and at them with no fear of the result." Accordingly, going out by the palisade gate and by the first gate in the long wall that then existed, he ran at full speed along the straight road, where the trophy now stands as you go past the steepest part of the hill. He fell on the center of the Athenians and routed them, panic-stricken by their own disorder and astounded at his audacity. At the same moment Clearidas, in execution of his orders, came out of the Thracian gates to support him, and also attacked the enemy. The result was that the Athenians, suddenly and unexpectedly attacked on both sides, fell into confusion. Their left wing, toward Eion, which had already moved off some distance, at once broke and fled. Just as it was in full retreat and Brasidas was passing on to attack the right, he was wounded; but his fall was not noticed by the Athenians, since those near him took him up and carried him off the field. The Athenian right made a better stand. Cleon, who from the start had no thought of fighting, at once fled and was overtaken and killed by a Myrcinian targeteer. But his infantry, forming in close order on the hill, twice or three times repulsed the attacks of Clearidas, and did not finally give way until they were surrounded and routed by the missiles of the Myrcinian and Chalcidian horse and the targeteers. Now the whole Athenian army was in flight. Those who escaped being killed in the battle, or by the Chalcidian horse and the targeteers, dispersed among the hills and with difficulty made their way back to Eion. The men who had picked up and rescued Brasidas brought him into the town still breathing. He lived long enough to hear of his troops' victory, and not long afterwards died. The rest of the army returning with Clearidas from the pursuit stripped the dead and set up a trophy.

After this, all the allies attended in arms and buried Brasidas at public expense in the city, in front of what is now the marketplace. The Amphipolitans, having enclosed his tomb, have ever afterwards sacrificed to him as a hero, and have given him the honor of games and annual offerings. They made him the founder of their colony, and pulled down the Hagnonic monuments, obliterating everything that could be taken as a memorial of Hagnon's having founded the place. They considered Brasidas had been their preserver, and as they were now courting the alliance of Lacedaemon out of fear of Athens, in their present hostile relations with Athens they could no longer with the same advantage or satisfaction pay Hagnon his honors. They also gave the Athenians back their dead. About six hundred of the Athenians had fallen, and only seven of the enemy, since there had been no regular engagement, but the matter of accident and panic I have described. After taking up their dead, the Athenians sailed home, while Clearidas and his troops remained to settle matters at Amphipolis.

About the same time three Lacedaemonians — Ramphias, Autocharidas, and Epicydidas — led a reinforcement of nine hundred heavy infantry to the towns in the direction of Thrace. Arriving at Heraclea in Trachis, they reorganized matters there as they thought best. While they delayed there, this battle took place, and so the summer ended.

At the beginning of the following winter, Ramphias and his companions penetrated as far as Pierium in Thessaly. But as the Thessalians opposed their further advance, and Brasidas, whom they had come to reinforce, was dead, they turned back home. They thought the moment had passed: the Athenians had been defeated and were gone, and they themselves were not equal to carrying out Brasidas's designs. The main reason for their return, however, was that they knew that when they set out Lacedaemonian opinion had really been in favor of peace.

As it happened, immediately after the battle of Amphipolis and the retreat of Ramphias from Thessaly, both sides stopped pressing the war and turned their attention to peace. Athens had suffered severely at Delium, and again shortly afterwards at Amphipolis, and no longer had the confidence in her strength that had earlier made her refuse to negotiate, in the belief — inspired by her successes of the moment — that ultimate victory was hers. Besides, she was afraid that her allies, tempted by her setbacks, might rebel more widely, and she regretted having let go the splendid opportunity for peace that the Pylos affair had offered. Lacedaemon, on the other hand, found the war's course refuted her assumption that a few years of ravaging Attic land would be enough to overthrow Athenian power. She had suffered on the island a disaster previously unknown at Sparta. She saw her territory plundered from Pylos and Cythera. The Helots were deserting, and she lived in constant fear that those who remained in the Peloponnese would rely on those outside and seize the chance to renew their old attempts at revolution. On top of all this, as it happened, her thirty years' truce with the Argives was about to expire, and they refused to renew it unless Cynuria were given back to them. Fighting Argos and Athens at the same time seemed impossible. She also suspected some of the cities of the Peloponnese of intending to go over to the enemy — and that in fact was the case.

These considerations made both sides ready for an accommodation. The Lacedaemonians were probably the more eager, since they ardently desired to recover the men taken on the island — Spartans who belonged to the leading families and were therefore related to the governing body in Lacedaemon. Negotiations had begun immediately after their capture, but the Athenians, in their hour of triumph, would not consent to any reasonable terms. After their defeat at Delium, however, Lacedaemon, knowing they would now be more inclined to listen, at once concluded the year-long armistice, during which the two sides were to confer and see whether a longer settlement could be reached.

Now, however, after the Athenian defeat at Amphipolis and the deaths of Cleon and Brasidas — who had been the two principal opponents of peace on either side, the latter because of the success and honor war gave him, the former because he thought that, if peace were restored, his crimes would be more easily detected and his slanders less believed — the foremost candidates for power in each city desired peace more ardently than ever. These were Pleistoanax son of Pausanias, king of Lacedaemon, and Nicias son of Niceratus, the most successful general of his time. Nicias, while still fortunate and honored, wished to secure his good fortune, to obtain a present release from trouble for himself and his countrymen, and to hand down to posterity a name as an ever-successful statesman. He thought the way to do this was to keep out of danger and commit himself as little as possible to fortune — and that only peace made keeping out of danger possible. Pleistoanax, on his side, was attacked by his enemies over his restoration, and was regularly held up by them to the prejudice of his countrymen whenever any reverse befell them, on the grounds that his unjust restoration was the cause. The accusation was that he and his brother Aristocles had bribed the prophetess of Delphi to tell the Lacedaemonian deputations who successively arrived at the temple to bring home from abroad the seed of the demigod son of Zeus, otherwise they would have to plow with a silver plowshare. In this way, it was alleged, he had eventually induced the Lacedaemonians, in the nineteenth year of his exile in Lycaeum (where he had gone when banished on suspicion of having been bribed to retreat from Attica, and had built half his house within the sacred precinct of Zeus for fear of the Lacedaemonians), to restore him with the same dances and sacrifices with which they had instituted their kings on the first settlement of Lacedaemon. The smart of this accusation, and the thought that in peacetime no disaster could occur, and that once Lacedaemon had recovered her men there would be nothing for his enemies to take hold of (whereas while the war lasted the highest station must always bear the blame for whatever went wrong), made him ardently desire a settlement. Accordingly the winter was spent in conferences. As spring approached rapidly, the Lacedaemonians sent round orders to the cities to prepare for a fortified occupation of Attica, and held this as a sword over the Athenians to induce them to listen to their offers. At last, after many claims had been urged on either side at the conferences, a peace was agreed on the following basis. Each side was to restore its conquests, but Athens was to keep Nisaea. Her demand for Plataea was countered by the Thebans' assertion that they had acquired the place not by force or treachery, but by the voluntary adhesion of its citizens by agreement — the same, according to the Athenian account, being the history of her acquisition of Nisaea. With this settled, the Lacedaemonians summoned their allies, and when all voted for peace except the Boeotians, Corinthians, Eleans, and Megarians, who did not approve of the proceedings, they concluded the treaty and made peace, each of the contracting parties swearing to the following articles:
The Athenians and Lacedaemonians and their allies made a treaty, and swore to it, city by city, as follows:

1. Concerning the national temples, there shall be free passage by land and by sea for all who wish to sacrifice, travel, consult, and attend the oracle or the games, according to the customs of their countries.

2. The temple and shrine of Apollo at Delphi, and the Delphians, shall be governed by their own laws, taxed by their own state, and judged by their own judges — the land and the people, according to the custom of their country.
3. The treaty shall be binding for fifty years upon the Athenians and their allies, and upon the Lacedaemonians and their allies, without fraud or harm by land or by sea.

4. It shall not be lawful to take up arms, with intent to do harm, either for the Lacedaemonians and their allies against the Athenians and their allies, or for the Athenians and their allies against the Lacedaemonians and their allies, in any way or by any means whatsoever. Should any dispute arise between them, they are to have recourse to law and oaths, in such form as may be agreed between the parties.

5. The Lacedaemonians and their allies shall give back Amphipolis to the Athenians. In the case of cities given up by the Lacedaemonians to the Athenians, however, the inhabitants shall be allowed to go where they please and to take their property with them. The cities shall be independent, paying only the tribute of Aristides. It shall not be lawful for the Athenians or their allies to make war on them after the treaty is concluded, so long as the tribute is paid. The cities in question are Argilus, Stagirus, Acanthus, Scolus, Olynthus, and Spartolus. These cities shall be neutral, allies of neither the Lacedaemonians nor the Athenians. But if the cities themselves consent, the Athenians may make them their allies, provided always that the cities wish it. The Mecybernaeans, Sanaeans, and Singaeans shall inhabit their own cities, as shall also the Olynthians and Acanthians. The Lacedaemonians and their allies shall give back Panactum to the Athenians.

6. The Athenians shall give back Coryphasium, Cythera, Methana, and any Lacedaemonians in the prison at Athens or elsewhere in the Athenian dominions. They shall let go the Peloponnesians besieged in Scione, and all others in Scione who are allies of the Lacedaemonians, and all whom Brasidas sent in there, and any other allies of the Lacedaemonians who may be in the prison at Athens or elsewhere in the Athenian dominions.
7. The Lacedaemonians and their allies shall in the same way give back any of the Athenians or their allies whom they hold.
8. In the case of Scione, Torone, Sermylium, and any other cities the Athenians may hold, the Athenians may adopt whatever measures they choose.

9. The Athenians shall take an oath to the Lacedaemonians and their allies, city by city. Every man shall swear by the most binding oath of his country, seventeen from each city. The oath shall be as follows: "I will abide by this agreement and treaty honestly and without deceit." In the same way an oath shall be taken by the Lacedaemonians and their allies to the Athenians. The oath shall be renewed annually by both parties. Pillars shall be erected at Olympia, Pythia, the Isthmus, at Athens on the Acropolis, and at Lacedaemon in the temple at Amyclae.

10. If anything be forgotten, whatever it be, and on whatever point, it shall be consistent with their oath for both parties, the Athenians and Lacedaemonians, to alter it, according to their discretion.

The treaty begins from the ephoralty of Pleistolas in Lacedaemon, on the 27th day of the month of Artemisium, and from the archonship of Alcaeus at Athens, on the 25th day of the month of Elaphebolion. Those who took the oath and poured the libations for the Lacedaemonians were Pleistoanax, Agis, Pleistolas, Damagetis, Chionis, Metagenes, Acanthus, Daithus, Ischagoras, Philocharidas, Zeuxidas, Antippus, Tellis, Alcinadas, Empedias, Menas, and Laphilus. For the Athenians: Lampon, Isthmonicus, Nicias, Laches, Euthydemus, Procles, Pythodorus, Hagnon, Myrtilus, Thrasycles, Theagenes, Aristocrates, Iolcius, Timocrates, Leon, Lamachus, and Demosthenes.

This treaty was made in the spring, just at the end of winter, directly after the city festival of Dionysus — exactly ten years, give or take a few days, from the first invasion of Attica and the start of this war. This must be calculated by the seasons rather than by trusting the enumeration of the names of the various magistrates or offices of honor that are commonly used to mark past events. Accuracy is impossible there, since an event may have occurred at the beginning, the middle, or any other point in a magistrate's term. But by counting in summers and winters, the method adopted in this history — each of these amounting to half a year — it will be found that there were ten summers and as many winters contained in this first war.

Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians, whose lot it was to begin the work of restitution, immediately set free all the prisoners of war they held, and sent Ischagoras, Menas, and Philocharidas as envoys to the towns in the direction of Thrace, with orders to Clearidas to hand over Amphipolis to the Athenians, and to the rest of their allies each to accept the treaty as it concerned them. The allies, however, did not like its terms and refused to accept it. Clearidas, too, willing to oblige the Chalcidians, would not hand over the town, claiming that he was unable to do so against their will. Meanwhile he hurried in person to Lacedaemon with envoys from the place, to defend his disobedience against possible charges from Ischagoras and his companions, and also to see whether it was too late for the agreement to be changed. Finding the Lacedaemonians were bound, he quickly set out back again, with their instructions to hand over the place if possible, or in any case to bring out the Peloponnesians who were in it.

The allies happened to be present in person at Lacedaemon, and those who had not accepted the treaty were now asked by the Lacedaemonians to adopt it. They again refused, however, for the same reasons as before, unless fairer terms than these were agreed on. Remaining firm in their decision, they were dismissed by the Lacedaemonians, who now decided to form an alliance with the Athenians. They reasoned that Argos — which had refused the application of Ampelidas and Lichas for a renewal of the treaty — would without Athens no longer be formidable, and that the rest of the Peloponnese would be most likely to keep quiet if the coveted alliance with Athens were closed off to them. Accordingly, after conference with the Athenian ambassadors, an alliance was agreed on and oaths were exchanged on the following terms:
1. The Lacedaemonians shall be allies of the Athenians for fifty years.

2. Should any enemy invade the territory of Lacedaemon and harm the Lacedaemonians, the Athenians shall help in whatever way they can most effectively, according to their power. But if the invader has gone after plundering the country, that city shall be the enemy of Lacedaemon and Athens, and shall be punished by both, and neither shall make peace without the other. This shall be done honestly, loyally, and without fraud.

3. Should any enemy invade the territory of Athens and harm the Athenians, the Lacedaemonians shall help them in whatever way they can most effectively, according to their power. But if the invader has gone after plundering the country, that city shall be the enemy of Lacedaemon and Athens, and shall be punished by both, and neither shall make peace without the other. This shall be done honestly, loyally, and without fraud.
4. Should the slave population rise, the Athenians shall help the Lacedaemonians with all their might, according to their power.

5. This treaty shall be sworn to by the same persons on either side who swore to the other. It shall be renewed annually by the Lacedaemonians going to Athens for the Dionysia, and the Athenians going to Lacedaemon for the Hyacinthia. A pillar shall be set up by either party: at Lacedaemon near the statue of Apollo at Amyclae, and at Athens on the Acropolis near the statue of Athene. Should the Lacedaemonians and Athenians see fit to add to or take away from the alliance in any particular, it shall be consistent with their oaths for both parties to do so, according to their discretion.

Those who took the oath for the Lacedaemonians were Pleistoanax, Agis, Pleistolas, Damagetus, Chionis, Metagenes, Acanthus, Daithus, Ischagoras, Philocharidas, Zeuxidas, Antippus, Alcinadas, Tellis, Empedias, Menas, and Laphilus. For the Athenians: Lampon, Isthmionicus, Laches, Nicias, Euthydemus, Procles, Pythodorus, Hagnon, Myrtilus, Thrasycles, Theagenes, Aristocrates, Iolcius, Timocrates, Leon, Lamachus, and Demosthenes.

This alliance was made not long after the treaty. The Athenians gave back the men from the island to the Lacedaemonians, and the summer of the eleventh year began. This completes the account of the first war, which occupied the entire ten years preceding.
